item.title: Canary - v2.3.3 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
* The ValueSetter module can now switch on the job keys that only settle once a search has finished, for example `$results.count$` in an `if.*` param. Previously a ValueSetter like `if.$results.count$=0` evaluated only once, so it permanently reported the initial value. Such a module now waits for the job to finish before pushing to its downstream modules. Keys that are meant to be read while a search is still running, like `$results.doneProgress$`, are unaffected and continue to push immediately, as does `$results.fields$`, which comes from the Fields module rather than from the job. * Fixed a bug in the parsing of search expressions, when a tab or a newline character was read as part of the field name next to it, rather than as the token separator that SPL treats it as. A search filter of " foo\=bar" would give you a field name with a tab character in it, and any SPL built from that field name was then invalid. * Canary no longer reads the operating system certificate store when it asks splunkd for search job status. On a machine that has a truncated or corrupt cert in the store, this problem caused every page used to silently stop updating. * Improved messaging to the user if our job status poller's python handler hits an unexpected exception. * Job status polling now keeps its connection to splunkd open between polls instead of negotiating a new TLS session for every one. This only takes about 3ms off each poll but in aggregate from many users it's worth doing.


Description:
Canary is essentially an alternate User Interface framework for Splunk. It implements its own extensible view creation slash dashboarding system that other apps can use. It is a descendant of the old Sideview Utils (defunct for years now) but whereas Sideview Utils ran on top of Splunk’s “Advanced XML” systems, Canary does not. For a great deal more information about Canary, see our website ( https://sideviewapps.com/documentation/canary ) NOTE: This app runs in python3 without any problems and without any changes required. Splunk's "Upgrade Readiness App" may erroneously state that our apps do not run in python3 but it is wrong and please contact us if you have any questions about this.

Short Description:
Build, import, validate, and package Splunk add-ons through a visual browser UI — no CLI. Create inputs (REST/shell/Python), alert actions, source types, field extractions, CIM mappings, lookups, and setup pages on the UCC Framework, run inputs and alerts in the browser to inspect their output, validate with AppInspect, and package for Splunkbase in one click.


Description:
TA Studio is a browser-based visual workbench for building Splunk® add-ons (TAs) on the Universal Configuration Console (UCC) Framework — without touching the command line. Authoring a quality add-on normally means working with the ucc-gen CLI, hand-editing globalConfig.json and a web of .conf files, and running AppInspect and packaging from a terminal. TA Studio replaces that workflow with a guided, point-and-click interface that runs entirely inside your own Splunk instance. From one UI you can create and manage data inputs (REST API, shell command, or Python modular inputs), alert actions (including Enterprise Security adaptive response), source types, field extractions with a live regex builder, CIM data model mappings, setup pages (accounts, proxy, logging), CSV lookups, and event types. You can import existing Splunk Add-on Builder and conf-based add-ons to modernize them, run inputs and alert actions right in the browser to inspect the events and output they produce, validate with AppInspect (including cloud checks) and review the results, then package a Splunkbase-ready archive in one click. TA Studio also includes built-in AI assistance to help you generate and refine input and alert-action code as you work. It otherwise runs entirely within your local Splunk environment: your add-on projects are not collected, transmitted, or stored outside your instance, and AI features send only the content you choose to submit to your selected AI provider.

item.title: WithSecure Elements Add-on - v1.1.1 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
## Release notes — v1.1.1 **Enhancement release on the 1.1.x line** — targets Splunk Enterprise / Cloud 10.2+ (Python 3.13). Same fix backported to the 1.0.x maintenance line as v1.0.8. ### What changed The WithSecure Elements API now returns a top-level `mitre` array on each BCD detection that mixes ATT\&CK tactic IDs (TA\*) and technique IDs (T\*), e.g. `["TA0003", "T1518.001", "T1543.002", "T1059.004"]`. Previously only the `activityContext[].mitre_id` items were populated for cloud detections and the flattened `ac_mitre_id` field was aliased to `mitre_technique_id`. Two new search-time EVAL calculated fields on the `withsecure:epp:bcd_detection` sourcetype split the flat array by prefix: ``` EVAL-mitre_technique_id = coalesce(mvfilter(match('mitre{}', "^T[0-9]")), ac_mitre_id) EVAL-mitre_tactic_id = mvfilter(match('mitre{}', "^TA[0-9]")) ``` The regexes are disjoint: `TA0003` matches `^TA[0-9]` but not `^T[0-9]` because `[0-9]` requires a digit at position 1, and `A` is not a digit. `mitre_technique_id` falls back to the legacy `ac_mitre_id` when the top-level array is not present, so events indexed before the API migration keep working. `mitre_tactic_id` is a new field aligned with the Splunk CIM Endpoint datamodel, no legacy fallback needed. ### SOC-friendly queries this enables ``` index=main sourcetype="withsecure:epp:bcd_detection" mitre_tactic_id="TA0003" index=main sourcetype="withsecure:epp:bcd_detection" mitre_technique_id IN ("T1059.001","T1112") index=main sourcetype="withsecure:epp:bcd_detection" | stats count by mitre_tactic_id mitre_technique_id ``` ### Upgrade safety Non-destructive in-place upgrade. Search-time only — no ingestion impact, applies retroactively to detections already in the index, 100 % reversible.


Short Description:
Collects EPP Security Events and EDR Broad Context Detections from WithSecure Elements via OAuth2-authenticated API, with CIM-compliant field extractions for endpoint, malware, intrusion detection, and process data.


Description:
The WithSecure Elements Add-on collects endpoint protection and detection data from the WithSecure Elements API. It ingests EPP Security Events and EDR Broad Context Detections through OAuth2-authenticated modular inputs, enabling centralized security event analysis in Splunk. The add-on maps collected events to CIM endpoint, malware, intrusion detection, and process tags, facilitating correlation with other security data sources. Two modular inputs handle data collection: withsecure_epp_input retrieves endpoint protection events, while withsecure_bcd_input collects EDR broad context detection incidents. Events are indexed under source types withsecure:epp:security_event, withsecure:epp:bcd_incident, and withsecure:epp:bcd_detection. The add-on includes a custom search command for retrieving specific detection details and provides a workflow action to fetch incident detections directly from the Splunk interface.

When a saved search triggers, EventTimeline creates a normalized finding containing the alert context, actor, resource, source IP, account, API action, severity, and event timestamp. Analysts can then fetch related CloudTrail activity for a selected investigation window and review what happened before, during, and after the alert. Description:
Sandfly is an agentless intrusion detection and incident response platform for Linux. Sandfly automatically analyzes Linux hosts for intruders 24 hours a day without loading any software on your endpoints. Additionally, Sandfly can retrieve hardware, operating system and related data for analysis in Splunk. Sandfly works across virtually all Linux distributions immediately without risk to stability or performance. The Sandfly Security Add-on for Splunk is a technology add-on that ingests events from a Sandfly Security server using the Sandfly Security REST API. item.title: Riskability - v1.2.3 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
# Riskability 1.2.3 Everything since 1.0.2, which is the version currently on this listing. 1.2.1, 1.2.2 and 1.2.3 add what is listed at the end. Only the changes that matter to somebody running the app are listed. ## A page about one machine Host detail gathers what the app knows about a single system, built as a dossier rather than a smaller copy of the fleet page. Identity and four clocks in one card: when the collector last ran, when the software last changed, when the host was last compared to the feed, and how old the feed is. Then an assessment ledger of what has been measured and what has not, what to do first, the open findings, the configuration surface the machine is set up to run, what it exposes, its Windows patch level, and what on it is no longer supported. The ledger is deliberately not a score. Its inputs are missing at unrelated rates, so a score would have to treat missing as zero, which is forbidden, or normalise over what is present, which is monotone the wrong way: the fewer things measured about a host, the better it would score. ## When nobody is going to fix it again The bundle now carries product and operating system support lifecycles, so the app can report software that has run out of supported releases. This is a different question from a CVE and no advisory answers it. Support is decided by who ships the copy. A package a distribution installs and maintains is informational while that distribution still supports its release, because vendors backport without changing the upstream version. A package carrying an esm or fips marker in its version string says in its own version that it is being maintained past the ordinary date. A copy no package manager owns is where the upstream date is the whole truth, and only that is reported at high confidence. A timeline on the Coverage page places every product release found on the fleet at the date its support ends, with everything already past that date included, because a product nobody has fixed for three years is the urgent end of the same timeline. Every row also states how much evidence there is that the software runs, from listening on a routable address down to installed with nothing observed running it. That order ranks evidence, not danger. Clicking a product on the timeline lists every host carrying it, and a row there opens that machine's own page. The lifecycle source is offered on both feed paths: a checkbox on the direct fetch in Feed administration, and a --lifecycle-file flag for a copy downloaded on a machine with better connectivity. Lifecycle data describes applications, runtimes, databases, servers and operating system releases rather than every library a distribution ships, so it covers a minority of any inventory and the Coverage page says so. ## Windows patch level, from Microsoft's own data A Windows host can now be told which build the vendor currently ships for its release, which update produces that build, and how many revisions behind it is. Windows 11 25H2 shipping as an enablement package over 24H2, and build 26100 being both Windows 11 24H2 and Server 2025, are both handled explicitly. The panel says current with the feed rather than up to date, and means it: the comparison is inside the host's own servicing branch and edition, so it is never a claim that the release itself is the newest one or is still supported. ## The Riskability Cycle The landing page shows what the app is doing right now and what it does next. Almost every schedule in Riskability runs hourly, so the panel is a dial: one turn is one cycle of the pipeline. The centre names the next job and counts down to it, the hand marks where in the hour you are, and the lit arc covers the stretch the app is actually working, which on a default install is :05 to :55. Around the ring is a mark for each scheduled job at its own minute, coloured by how it last finished, and naming itself, its minute and its last duration when hovered. They are deliberately texture rather than a list: which of thirty six runs next matters far less than whether the cycle is turning at all, and a failure shows as a red mark on the ring without needing to be picked out by name. The two schedules that are not hourly cannot sit on an hour dial, so they are named underneath with when they next run rather than being left out. The panel refreshes every minute, so the countdown is live without reloading the page. It reads Splunk's own REST endpoints for the schedules and their last runs, and needs no access to any index, so it works for an account that can see the app but not the internal logs. An account that cannot see the schedules at all is told so, rather than being shown an idle pipeline. ## Hosts that are quiet on purpose A host that has not reported for a month is not necessarily broken. Some are collected only after a deliberate change. The app now learns each host's own reporting rhythm and calls it late only against that, rather than against a fixed threshold. Learned rhythms in testing ranged from hourly to once every sixty two days. Hosts that had gone quiet were previously deleted from the app outright and are now kept. ## Findings that were never real Installer and launcher stubs were catalogued as the software they install, producing findings about software that was not present. Load evidence could cross root boundaries, matching a snap base's library against the host's copy of the same name. On Windows a doubled backslash in a path meant a package could never be recognised as fixed, so an upgraded package stayed open forever. Open findings on the test fleet fell from 5,340 to 2,688, and none of the difference was a vulnerability that stopped being reported. A finding is also closed only when the source that reported it actually ran again. A collector invoked with a narrower set of sources no longer reads as software having been removed. ## Colour that means the same on every chart Chart colour was relative to whatever was on screen, so a fleet whose worst case was four findings and one whose worst case was four thousand drew the same picture. Colour is now an absolute scale, and a pale chart is a statement rather than an accident. ## Tables Date columns take a real range: an exact day, since, before, a span such as 2026-08-01..2026-08-28, and open ended forms such as 2026-08-01 followed by two dots. Columns whose values are typed rather than chosen no longer offer a dropdown of every value in the column. Advisories that never received a CVE number, such as GHSA, USN, DSA and RHSA identifiers, are links rather than plain text. ## Upgrading Replace the app and reload. No configuration changes and nothing to do on the forwarders or the indexers. The Windows patch level and end of support panels are populated by the next feed you import and say so until then, rather than implying that everything is current and supported. ## Corrections in 1.2.1 The support timeline's look ahead window and product picker are inside that panel now, rather than in a filter bar that implied it filtered the whole page. Every source in a bundle declares itself in the sources table on Feed administration. Windows update history registered nothing before, so a bundle carrying Microsoft build data did not say so and its attribution was recorded nowhere. The lifecycle source is named for its publisher, endoflife-date, like every other row there. ## Corrections in 1.2.2 Feed administration reported the Windows update source as unreachable when it was not. Every source was probed with an HTTP HEAD request, and Microsoft's update index answers HEAD with 405 Method Not Allowed while answering the request the builder actually makes with 200. Anyone reading that would have concluded Windows patch data could not be fetched and left it out. A source that refuses HEAD is now asked again the way the real fetch asks. ## Corrections in 1.2.3 A host is now kept for 180 days without contact rather than 30. That setting, `riskability_host_retire_days`, is the only thing deciding how long silence is tolerated, and a month deleted exactly the estates this app is built for: an appliance or OT fleet collected once a quarter lost every host between scans and was rediscovered later as new machines with no history. Lower it if your hosts report nightly, raise it for an annual audit cycle. Three tiles on the landing page stopped colouring themselves as faults. Newest inventory turned amber after six hours and red after forty eight, which tells a fleet collected twice a week that it is failing while it does exactly what it was configured to do. Last match climbed for ever on a stable fleet, because nothing is compared when nothing new has arrived, so it went red for having nothing to do. Open findings was amber above one finding and red above a hundred, which is every real fleet, permanently. All three are answered properly elsewhere: whether a host is late is judged against its own learned rhythm, and whether the pipeline is running is shown directly by the cycle dial. Feed age keeps its colour, because a stale feed does degrade every answer on every page no matter how often anybody scans. A host that reports rarely no longer disappears. Three views rebuilt themselves from a thirty day window and replaced their contents wholesale, so a machine quieter than that dropped out of the end of support view, the Windows patch level and the ecosystem coverage panel entirely, and the page then read as an answer rather than as missing data. They now carry their state forward like the rest of the app, and a single setting, riskability_host_retire_days, decides how long a silent host is kept. It defaults to thirty days and a site whose hosts report quarterly should raise it. There is no minimum collection frequency, and the Details tab now says so along with the smallest flag set the app can use. This matters for appliance and OT estates that are collected only after a deliberate change, which are a first class case here rather than an edge case. The feed builder can also be handed a source that the search head cannot download. Feed administration previously told anyone blocked from CISA to rebuild the entire bundle offline, which meant downloading every other source again over one file. A blocked source can now be uploaded on the page and the direct fetch uses it while downloading the rest as normal.


Short Description:
Correlate the software your fleet already reports against offline CVE databases on a search head with no internet access. Ranks findings by exploitation likelihood and by whether the network can actually reach them. Track software that is already or soon becoming End Of Life!


Description:
Most vulnerability tooling cannot run where it is needed most. A search head with no route to the internet cannot call an API, pull a feed on a schedule, or fetch a score on demand. Riskability is built for that machine. It takes the software inventory your hosts already report, correlates it against vulnerability databases you carry across the air gap yourself, and answers what a CVE count never does: of everything found, what should somebody actually do tonight? THE PROBLEM A fleet of any size produces tens of thousands of open findings. Severity alone does not reduce that to a working list. CVSS describes how bad a vulnerability would be if exploited, not how likely anyone is to exploit it, and neither knows whether your copy is reachable. WHAT THIS APP ADDS Exploitation likelihood. Findings are ranked by EPSS, the published probability that a vulnerability will be exploited in the wild, and by the CISA KEV catalogue of vulnerabilities already observed under exploitation. Both arrive in the feed you import, never fetched live. Reachability. The collector reports listening ports, the process holding each one, and the containers behind them. Riskability separates findings that answer a network address from those that answer only loopback, and from those with nothing listening at all. On a test fleet that turned 10,206 open findings into 11 that answer the network. It reorders the work. It never shortens it. End of support. A CVE says a thing is broken. End of support says nobody is going to fix it again, which no advisory states. Product and operating system lifecycles ride in the same bundle, so the app names software that has run out of supported releases, places each on a timeline at the date support ends, and says how much evidence there is that it runs. One machine at a time. A host page gathers what is known about a single system: what has been measured on it and what has not, what it runs, what it exposes, and its Windows patch level. WHAT IT REFUSES TO GUESS Every finding carries a confidence level, and confidence describes the strength of the evidence rather than the severity of the vulnerability. Ubuntu and Red Hat backport fixes without changing the upstream version, so a version comparison alone cannot settle whether such a package is patched. Riskability reports that as informational and says why. The same rule governs end of support: a package a distribution still maintains is not called abandoned because its upstream series finished. A Coverage dashboard lists what the imported data cannot speak to at all, because a gap in visibility is not an absence of risk. Accepted risks are recorded in an audit index that is written once and never rewritten: who accepted, when, why, and when the acceptance expires. NO OUTBOUND NETWORK ACCESS The app makes no outbound requests. You build a feed bundle on a connected machine with the builder the app hands you, carry it across, and import it. Nothing is scheduled at install time.

## Version 2.0.0 **Important — action required after upgrading.** Data inputs configured in v1.1.2 or earlier will no longer be listed on the Inputs page after this upgrade and must be recreated. Configured accounts, credentials and add-on settings are retained and do not need to be re-entered. ### Breaking change: modular input types renamed All modular input types are now prefixed with `vectra_rux_`: | Previous (v1.1.2 and earlier) | v2.0.0 and later | | --- | --- | | `entity_scoring_input` | `vectra_rux_entity_scoring_input` | | `detections_input` | `vectra_rux_detections_input` | | `audits_input` | `vectra_rux_audits_input` | | `lockdown_input` | `vectra_rux_lockdown_input` | | `health_input` | `vectra_rux_health_input` | Earlier releases used generic input-type names that other Splunk technology add-ons can also define. Modular input names are unique per Splunk instance, so where another add-on defined the same name, Splunk could load the wrong input definition or return an error on the Inputs page. Prefixing every Vectra input type guarantees these definitions are unique. Splunk treats the renamed types as new inputs, which is why data inputs created in v1.1.2 or earlier are not carried forward. ### New features * **Detection input** — added `Include Triaged`, `Include Info Category` and `From Checkpoint ID`. `From Checkpoint ID` lets collection begin from a specific detection event ID on the first run. * **Health input** — added optional collection of EDR and external connector health data: `Get Health EDR`, `Get Health EDR Details`, `Get Health External Connectors` and `Get Health External Connectors Details`. Each dataset is ingested with its own `source` value so it can be searched independently. ### Changes * Detection, audit and lockdown collection migrated to Vectra RUX API v3.5. Health and entity scoring collection continues to use v3.4. * Entity scoring collects from the unified `/entities` endpoint using page-based pagination. * The add-on version reported to the Vectra API is now read from `app.conf` at runtime, so it stays accurate across releases. * Refreshed Vectra branding for the app icon and navigation logo. ### Upgrade procedure 1. Record the configuration of each existing data input (name, interval, index and Vectra RUX account). 2. Disable & delete all configured inputs. 3. Install the v2.0.0 package with the **Upgrade app** option selected. 4. Restart Splunk. A restart is required for this release. 5. Recreate each data input from the Inputs page using the values recorded in step 1. Existing checkpoints are preserved. Recreating an input with the same name resumes collection from where it stopped, avoiding gaps and duplicate events. ### Documentation * [Upgrade guide: v1.1.2 to v2.0.0](https://docs.vectra.ai/configuration/response/siem/upgrade-guide-vectra-xdr-technology-add-on-v1.1.2-to-vectra-rux-technology-add-on-v2.0.0) * [Splunk On-Prem integration guide](https://docs.vectra.ai/configuration/response/siem/splunk-siem-vectra-integration-guide-start-here-for-rux) * [Splunk Cloud integration guide](https://docs.vectra.ai/configuration/response/siem/splunk-siem-vectra-integration-guide-start-here-for-rux-1) ### Support Email [support@vectra.ai](mailto:support@vectra.ai)

item.title: Adjutant AI (AI Workbench) - v2.4.0 [New App Release]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
# Adjutant AI (formerly AI Workbench) — Release notes What's new, improved, and fixed in each release, in plain language. This is the **customer-facing** summary used for the Splunkbase release-notes section; the full technical changelog lives in the project's detailed release notes. **Last updated:** 2026-08-26 > **About version numbers.** Releases once numbered 0.10–0.13 were renumbered to > 1.0–1.3 to reflect production maturity — no behaviour changed. The current release is > **2.4.0** — a connectivity release on top of **2.2.2**, itself a maintenance release on **2.2.1**, itself a maintenance release on > **2.2.0**'s **Explain a SPL search**, and **2.1.0**'s **Fraud capability** and the **2.0 line** (the deterministic **ITSI Root > Cause Analysis** engine, **resource-consumption monitoring**, and **2.0.7**'s durable memory, > Scheduled Ask and governed integrations), which in turn built on > **1.8.5** (the **CIM Coverage Audit**), **1.8.4** (async playbook execution over MCP > plus the **Outcome Ledger** executive/audit dashboard), **1.8.3** > (a security‑hardening release: OWASP + dependency + anti‑ransomware audit), **1.8.2** (Splunk > Edge Processor data‑quality awareness and keyless Azure OpenAI authentication), **1.8.1** > (support‑diagnosis fixes) and **1.8.0** (agent telemetry & OCSF export, content packs, > all‑tiers data‑quality checks, Splunk 10.x readiness, Dashboard Studio version‑awareness). The > **1.7.0** ServiceNow integration and the **1.5.0 "Data Foundation & MCP OAuth"** themes are > included below. --- ## 2.4.0 "Getting connected" Everything here came out of two customer setups in the same fortnight: an Azure OpenAI service published through a corporate API gateway, and one behind a private endpoint. Both stalled in the same place. The credentials were right, the firewall was open, the built-in connection test was green — and every question still failed. The release is about closing the distance between "the test passes" and "it works", and about not making an administrator assemble a URL by hand from three values nobody gave them. ### Find my endpoint (Azure OpenAI) Azure needs the complete address of a deployment, not the address of the service: everything up to and including `/chat/completions`, with the deployment name and an api-version in it. Behind a gateway that address also carries a path prefix chosen by whoever publishes the API. An administrator is typically handed a base URL and expected to work out the other three parts, and getting any of them wrong produces a "Resource not found" that reads like a permissions problem. There is now a **Find my endpoint** button beneath the endpoint field. Give it whatever you were given — often just the hostname — and it works out the rest from the Splunk server itself, then offers to fill in the endpoint, the deployment and the api-version in one click. Where the service lists its deployments, it also shows you every deployment it found together with the model behind each one, which answers a question customers ask constantly: the deployment is named `gpt-4o`, but is that actually what runs? It finds the address by paying attention to *how* each attempt is refused rather than just that it failed. A gateway refusing an address it does not publish answers differently from Azure refusing a deployment name it does not have, and the second kind of refusal proves the rest of the address is already right. When it cannot finish the job it says exactly what is still missing instead of failing vaguely — most usefully "the address and version are confirmed, the deployment name is not", which turns a five-part question for the API team into a one-part question. It also recognises a service that speaks the OpenAI dialect rather than the Azure one, and tells you to change provider instead of leaving you to guess. It runs only when you press it, and it is capped so it cannot flood anyone's gateway. ### Test connection now reports on the address, not just the login The connection test could report success on a configuration that no question would ever work against. It checked whether the credential was accepted, and an address that answers "not found" still accepts a credential — so a wrong address passed the test and failed every time it was used. That combination sent at least one administrator hunting through firewall rules for an afternoon. It now reports the two things separately. When the address does not work it says so plainly, and distinguishes the two reasons — an address that was left as the service base, or a deployment name that does not exist. When everything is right, it names the model that answered. ### Proxy exceptions, per configuration Reaching Microsoft to sign in and reaching the AI service are two different destinations, and in a locked-down network they often need opposite treatment: the corporate proxy is the only way out to Microsoft, while the service itself answers only on a direct connection. Until now a configuration had one proxy setting for both, so whichever you chose broke the other, and the only workaround changed proxy behaviour for every Splunk process on the machine. Configurations that use a proxy can now list the hosts that must bypass it. Sign-in goes through the proxy, the AI service is reached directly, nothing else on the server is affected, and the change takes effect when you save rather than when you restart. ### Fixed - **Model discovery found nothing behind an API gateway.** The lookup rebuilt the address from the hostname alone and threw away the path prefix, so it asked the wrong place and quietly reported no models. It now keeps the prefix. - **Deployments with your own naming lost their cost figures.** A deployment named for your estate rather than for the model — `acme-gpt4o-prod` — is not a name the price list knows, so usage was recorded with no money against it. The model that actually answered is now recorded alongside the configured name and used for pricing when the configured name is unknown, so those deployments cost correctly. Where the two differ, both are kept. - **A licence that could never be activated said "re-activate".** A key issued with no device limit records no activations at all, so a node-locked tier can never be satisfied by it and pressing re-activate cannot help. The licence page now says the key was issued without a device limit and needs reissuing, instead of sending administrators round a loop that had no exit. --- ## 2.2.2 "Finish the dashboard" A maintenance release about one thing: runs that did all the work and then ended with nothing on the glass. Every item came from watching real dashboard builds on a live estate, and in each case the assistant's own safety check was the reason the dashboard never appeared. The check was right about the problem and wrong about what to do next — it refused, gave instructions, and the instructions either could not be carried out or cost more of the run's budget than was left. ### Fixed - **Dashboards that were refused are now repaired instead.** When two panels ran the same underlying search, the assistant used to stop and describe a three-step manual fix. The fix is mechanical, so the builder now performs it: it creates the shared search once, points both panels at it, and keeps the fields those panels need. Your dashboards get the efficient shape without the run being interrupted, and the same search no longer runs twice. - **Panels that came back empty next to a search that clearly had data.** When a shared search was widened more than once to serve different panels, each widening discarded the previous one. On one nine-panel dashboard five panels showed "No results found" while the search behind them returned the right events. The widenings now combine. - **A check that asked for the impossible.** A panel that calculates its own value — a formatted date, a derived score — was refused for not finding that value in the shared search, where it cannot exist, because the panel computes it afterwards. Values a panel makes for itself are no longer demanded of the search. The related guidance was also wrong in a way that mattered: panels sharing a search are siblings, not a sequence, so a value one panel calculates is invisible to the others and has to be calculated where all of them can see it. - **A failed publish threw away the work it told you to fix.** The message on a validation failure said the dashboard was still open for editing and warned against starting over. It had in fact been discarded, so the repair failed and the assistant rebuilt every panel from scratch — which on one run quietly changed a correct detection into a different one. The dashboard now genuinely stays open when publishing fails. - **One special character could cost an entire dashboard.** A "≥" written as `≥` in a panel's explanatory text made the whole dashboard invalid, discarding a run of around forty steps that had already produced four working searches. Special characters in text are now handled safely no matter which one is used. - **An empty shared-search reference was treated as a real one**, producing a confusing refusal at publish time that asked for a search with a blank name. ### Improved - **Detections are now held to what you asked for.** New guidance covers the ways a detection can look perfect and point at the wrong event — quietly matching a wider set of events than you described, being loosened until it finally returns a row, discarding the field that distinguishes one event type from another, or dropping the amounts and account numbers an analyst needs before the result reaches the table. A rule that renders beautifully and flags the wrong event is worse than one that returns nothing, because nothing looks broken and nobody checks. The assistant now reads its own result back against the raw events before handing it to you. - **"No results" is no longer accepted as proof a detection works.** For a rule whose job is to match something, an empty result proves only that the syntax is valid — "this does not happen in your data" and "this rule cannot detect it" look identical. The assistant now establishes which of the two it is found before telling you, and runs over a period that actually covers the evidence it has already located. - **Sequence detections ("A, then B, then C") are built correctly.** A common shortcut for expressing order silently sorts alphabetically instead of by time, which can make a rule return nothing on a textbook-perfect match. Ordering is now derived from timestamps. ### Changed - **"Create / Update user template" are now "Create / Update user playbook"**, matching the Playbooks tab they belong to. Existing private playbooks you authored are unaffected; the old entries are retired so you are not offered both. --- ## 2.2.1 "Proven" A maintenance release, and every item in it came from running 2.2.0 against a real estate rather than from reading the code. One new capability came along with the fixes. ### Fraud rings your risk threshold cannot see (Enterprise, fraud-analytics) Risk-based alerting adds up one entity's score across many events. A fraud ring is the opposite shape: many entities sharing one thing. Because those are different questions, no amount of threshold tuning finds a ring. Seventeen mule accounts each earning fifteen points against a threshold of forty are seventeen well-behaved customers, since the risk was split seventeen ways and no single account ever crossed. Lower the threshold and you get seventeen false positives, not one ring. This release adds the query that asks the other question: group by the shared attribute instead of by the account. Nothing new has to be collected, because fraud risk rules have always recorded the linking attribute alongside the score. It simply was never read back this way. It is rarity-weighted, which matters more than it sounds. Ask only "what is shared" and the answer is always the corporate proxy that everybody sits behind. Shared attributes are ranked the same way the Fraud Ring Mapper ranks them, so a shared password hash and a shared IP are never treated as equal evidence, and values that are simply infrastructure are shown separately rather than quietly removed — a short list should not be mistaken for a clean estate. It is also honest about one thing it cannot know. It counts accounts that some rule already scored, which is not the same as how many accounts exist that share the value. So it hands you the search that settles it against your real data, and until you run that, it labels its own confidence as provisional instead of guessing. If you cannot name a starting account, the Fraud Ring Mapper will now find candidates for you before it starts walking. ### Fixed - **Money laundering was graded ready on two weeks of data.** Structuring is a run of individually unremarkable deposits and layering is a graph, so neither is visible in a short window however complete the feed is. Our own use case catalogue has always said to grade retention as well as fields; the grader printed that note and never acted on it. History is now graded, and a use case whose data does not go back far enough is capped at partial with the shortfall named. It is worth separating from other gaps, because it is the one you close with a retention policy rather than an onboarding project. On our demo estate this moved money laundering from ready to partial. - **Every ServiceNow tool call failed** with an internal error reference and no explanation. A tenant lookup returned a dictionary and the calling code expected a pair. - **The fraud readiness dashboard.** Four defects, found by running it rather than reading it. The readiness lookup was private to our own app, so when a dashboard was generated into a customer app the summary panel could not resolve it and rendered empty — which reads as "nothing has been graded" rather than "you cannot see it from here". The audit's own verdicts were being re-graded on the way to the screen, so nine computed verdicts became eight different ones. The coverage audit could not reach the dashboard builder at all, so nothing enforced that a panel must return data before it goes on the glass, and an empty panel on a fraud dashboard is read as "nothing wrong". And no fraud dashboard mentioned data quality: no ingestion check, no TrackMe, no Cribl or Edge Processor. A readiness grade computed over a feed that is arriving late or half delivered is a confident answer about the wrong data, and it fails towards "you are ready". That panel is now mandatory and appears even when everything is clean, because "we checked and it is healthy" is a finding. - **Asking for a readiness audit in plain English now reaches the readiness audit.** The question our own demo guide tells people to ask did not route to the playbook it names. - **Fraud verdict columns are coloured.** Ready, partial and blocked — and the feed inventory's present and absent — were missing from the status colour map, so those columns could only be coloured by hand and often were not. - **A dashboard opened from a finished session sat on "Loading..."** until you refreshed the tab. The new tab was sharing a browser process with a page that was still busy, so it never got a chance to start. - **The dashboard builder could refuse a fix it gave no way to make.** A publish refusal asked for a base search to be amended, and nothing could amend one, so the assistant looped between rebuilding and hand-editing. There is now a tool for it. - **The write-confirmation prompt asked about writes that could not succeed.** You were approving changes that validation then refused anyway. Validation now runs first, so the prompt only appears for writes that can actually happen. - **Token and cost accounting missed cached tokens.** With prompt caching the provider reports only the uncached part of the input, so an agentic run showed a few thousand tokens next to a cost that looked impossible. Cached tokens are now recorded, priced and shown. This affected what we reported, never what you were charged. - **Test Connection for Azure could only ever time out on a broken network.** Its own retries outlasted the window Splunk Web allows, so you got a bare 504 instead of the staged diagnostic. It now finishes inside the window and tells you which stage failed. ### Improved - **History groups by conversation.** A playbook run and its follow-up replies were listed as separate entries. They are now one entry with the turns nested inside and a combined cost. - **Large tool results no longer inflate every later call.** A stateless chat API re-sends the whole conversation on each tool round-trip, so one oversized result was paid for repeatedly. Results are now bounded before they enter the conversation. --- ## 2.2.0 "Explain" ### Explain a SPL search — free on every tier Point it at a search and get back an explanation you keep. Paste the SPL, name a saved search, or give it a dashboard and let it explain every panel. You get a private dashboard and a private saved search holding the same search fully commented, using native SPL comments so the commented copy is still a real, runnable search rather than a printout. This is on **every tier, including the free one**. Reading somebody else's search is the first thing a new Splunk user needs and the last thing they should have to pay for. **It explains what the search does here, not what the commands mean in general.** Your macros are expanded to their real definitions. `tag=web` is resolved to the eventtypes it actually selects on your system. Lookups are shown with their real columns. Command behaviour comes from your own installation's grammar, so an app-contributed command is described correctly. **And it runs the thing.** The pipeline is split at up to four points and each piece is executed over your sample window, so the walkthrough says "the base search returns 4,812 events with 14 extracted fields; after `stats count by host, status` that becomes 37 rows with 3 fields" using your real names and numbers. A field the SPL references that never appears in the results is flagged — the most common silent SPL bug, and one no text-only explainer can see. A search that returns nothing is bracketed to the stage where it broke. Nothing it could not verify is presented as if it were. Verified and unverified statements are never mixed together quietly. ### "Explain this" is usually "why did this stop working" Those two questions arrive in the same sentence, and reading SPL cannot tell them apart: a search whose data stopped arriving looks exactly like a search that was always wrong. So every run takes a feed verdict for the indexes involved, whether or not the search looked healthy. A source that stopped reporting half its hosts, or is arriving four hours late, still returns rows and still looks right — that is precisely when a check is worth having. Reads Cribl's own forwarded logs and metrics to surface the timestamp / parse / dropped-event problems that happen *inside Cribl, before Splunk can see them* — the "green in Splunk but timestamped wrong" blind spot — folded into one readiness verdict. No Cribl Lake or Search required. **New — LLM reliability: retry, fallback & circuit breaker** (Enterprise). A brief provider hiccup (503 / 529 / rate-limit) auto-retries within a time budget; a per-config **circuit breaker** stops hammering a provider that's down, then probes for recovery; and an ordered **fallback** transparently switches to your next provider (and tells you which it used). Two new admin dashboards — **LLM Health** and **AI Activity** — plus per-user / BU / org concurrency caps, all conservative and off the critical path. **New — live model & cost catalogue (all editions).** Models and prices come from a runtime catalogue that updates without an app rebuild; **automatic model discovery** (Professional+) keeps it current without ever logging your keys; an Enterprise admin screen adds price overrides and manual model registration for private gateways. **Fixed.** Generated Simple XML dashboards now share a single base search across panels (faster) and get a top data-ingestion health panel; corrected a 3× Opus price over-charge (now server-side authoritative, with Opus 4.8 and Fable 5 included). --- ## 1.5.0 "Data Foundation & MCP OAuth" **New:** connect to **OAuth 2.1‑protected MCP servers** (authorization‑code + PKCE for interactive, client‑credentials for unattended; tokens held server‑side, never in the browser — see [MCP_OAUTH.md](MCP_OAUTH.md)); **onboard new data sources** — describe a source or attach a sample file and get a deployment‑ready add‑on package; a **"is my data parsed correctly?"** ingestion/timestamp check that reads Splunk's own internal logs; generated config **validated against your instance** and given a **0–100 Data Quality Score** (A–F); and attach a local sample file in Ask (only the file name is audited, never contents). **Improved:** works with the newest OpenAI "reasoning" models incl. Azure GPT‑5.4 / GPT‑5.4‑mini (auto‑detects the request format); more reliable generated dashboards; generated objects use the **`aiworkbench`** name tag; and Audit‑tab improvements (Business Unit column/filter, local‑timezone timestamps, reliable token/outcome capture). --- ## Earlier releases (1.0.0 – 1.4.3) - **1.4.3** — Clearer guidance and plain-language fixes when a free-tier LLM key hits its provider limits (e.g. Groq token-per-minute caps, Gemini zero-quota keys); the LLM config screen flags these up front. - **1.4.1** — Per-feature capability licensing with edition badges (Professional / Enterprise / MSP); gated features show a padlock, and nothing you created is ever deleted when a tier changes. Turn-level audit logging made reliable; more robust dashboard generation. - **1.4.0** — The assistant reads your own Splunk **live** (real search commands + installed visualizations) instead of guessing; Splunk Security Essentials detection content integrated. - **1.3.3** — TrackMe integration end-to-end (feed-health awareness + actions) with richer built-in platform knowledge. - **1.3.2** — First Splunkbase 1.x release: packaging and permissions hardening. - **1.3.1** — Fixed Org/BU edits dropping fields; safeguard to keep bundled playbooks correct after upgrades. - **1.3.0** — Real, per-Organisation audit logging of every AI interaction (Professional+). - **1.2.0** — Splunk Security Essentials content tools for playbooks. - **1.1.1** — Cisco Deep Time Series Model (CDTSM) playbooks: pre-trained anomaly detection and forecasting via the AI Toolkit, each with a proof dashboard. - **1.1.0** — Multi-tenancy and the Organisation / Business-Unit editor overhauled for clearer, safer tenant scoping. - **1.0.0** — The knowledge layer: ground answers in your organisation's own conventions. *(Releases before 1.0 are early pre-release history and are omitted here.)* --- ## Known issues - **Open the assistant from inside another app.** Adjutant AI is a "host shell": reach it from a navigation-menu entry inside Search, Enterprise Security, ITSI, or your own apps — not by clicking the app tile directly. Everything it creates lands in the namespace of the app you opened it from. - **Some Data Foundation features need self-hosted Splunk.** The configuration-reference grounding and config-package generation (1.5.0) read files on the Splunk server, so they are unavailable on Splunk Cloud; the assistant says so and continues with what it can. --- *When a published fix resolves a tracked GitHub issue, it is summarised here with its issue number — for example: "Fixed: a dashboard panel could display raw HTML markup as text instead of formatting it (#123)."*


Short Description:
A workbench for Splunk, not just a chatbot. Analyse, correlate and build across SPL, dashboards, alerts, AI Toolkit / MLTK, ES, ITSI and TrackMe through tools that understand each one — plus any MCP server you add. Pick your LLM: Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure, Groq, Gemini, Bedrock, Ollama, OpenRouter. Multi-tenant, multi-tier (Free, Pro, Enterprise, MSP).


Description:
Adjutant AI (formerly AI Workbench) is a generative workspace for Splunk — not a chatbot bolted onto search, but a real workbench where you investigate, analyse and build with tools that understand Splunk. It is a host shell: it has no use-cases of its own, deriving everything from the Splunk app a user opens it from and their roles. Install once on the Search Head, then embed it in the apps your users already live in — Search, ITSI, Enterprise Security, your SOC and MSP customer apps. Users never leave the app they came from, and artefacts land in that app's namespace. Ask in plain English. Get back validated SPL, Simple XML and Dashboard Studio dashboards, alerts, lookups, reports and Splunk AI Toolkit (MLTK) machine-learning pipelines — grounded in your running Splunk (your knowledge objects, live command syntax, CIM models), run for real before they are saved, owned by the calling user. The depth is the difference. Where a generic MCP-only assistant talks to Splunk through one broad door, Adjutant AI ships fine-grained, Splunk-aware tools across Core, Enterprise Security, ITSI, TrackMe, ServiceNow and the AI Toolkit, each scoped to one job and run under your existing Splunk ACLs. Extend it with HTTP tools or any MCP server. New in 2.1 — a fraud capability that starts by telling you what you cannot yet detect. The Fraud Data Coverage Audit grades your estate against nine use cases (including AML) and returns ready, partial or blocked with the specific blocker, identifying event families by what events contain rather than by sourcetype name. Entity resolution runs before scoring, because risk accumulates per entity. Generated rules are weighted contributions with readable reasons, emitted into Enterprise Security's risk framework where it exists and into RBA's own field vocabulary where it does not. Nothing generated is ever enabled or scheduled. New in 2.0 — ITSI Root Cause Analysis with no LLM in the answer. It walks your real dependency graph, verifies the data behind every KPI, scores the evidence transparently, then lets an LLM narrate. The same evidence always gives the same answer. A red KPI on a dead feed is a data problem, and it names the forwarder, HEC, DB Connect, Cribl or Edge Processor leg at fault. Plus durable memory, scheduled playbooks, governed integrations, and per-tenant resource-consumption reporting. Your SOC can watch the agent: LLM calls, tool and ServiceNow calls, config changes, unattended verdicts and policy refusals emitted as OCSF events to an index Enterprise Security already watches. On-prem, no cloud egress, off by default. Bring your own LLM: Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Groq, Gemini, Bedrock, Ollama (fully offline) or OpenRouter — server-side, so keys never leave the search head. Multi-tenant by design. Free, Professional, Enterprise and MSP tiers, self-serve and air-gap-friendly.

Requires a free or paid [https://macadress.com](https://macadress.com) API key (https://macadress.com/signup) and outbound HTTPS access from the search head to [https://api.macadress.com.](https://api.macadress.com.)

Description:
TA-macadress adds a `macaddresslookup` search command that resolves MAC addresses to vendor, device category, virtualization, and special-use information, using the macadress.com API. Any event with a MAC address field, DHCP leases, ARP tables, wireless associations, switch port tables, asset inventories, can be enriched in place with: - Vendor and manufacturer identity, resolved against the full IEEE OUI registry (organization name, matched registry prefix, country) - Device category inference (router, switch, wireless access point, embedded device, and more) from a manually curated, source-verified dataset, not a guess - Virtualization and container detection: VMware, Hyper-V, Xen, VirtualBox, Parallels, QEMU/KVM, and Docker's default bridge convention - Special-use address classification: broadcast, IPv4/IPv6 multicast, VRRP, HSRP, STP, LACP, 802.1X, LLDP, each with its source protocol cited - Randomization signals: whether an address is locally administered or otherwise likely to be a privacy-randomized or spoofed MAC, useful for flagging anomalous device behavior in security and asset-inventory use cases This turns a raw MAC address into something you can actually search, filter, and stat on: `stats count by mac_organization`, `where mac_virtualization_platform!=""`, `where mac_potentially_randomized=1`, and so on, without leaving SPL. Lookups are batched (up to 100 addresses per API call) for efficiency on large event volumes, and the API key is stored via Splunk's encrypted storage/passwords endpoint rather than a plain-text configuration file. A free API key is available at macadress.com/signup; paid plans raise the request-rate and monthly-quota limits for larger deployments.

Release Notes:
# Release notes ## 4.0.0 **Minimum platform is now Splunk Enterprise / Splunk Cloud 10.4.** Version 3.1.0 stays available on Splunkbase for 9.x deployments and remains supported — 4.0.0 is the same app rebuilt around what Dashboard Studio 10.4 makes possible, not a different product. ### The headline: a segmentation map New **Segmentation Map** dashboard, built on the 10.4 network graph. The firewall log is the cheapest east-west flow evidence most estates have; this turns it into something you can act on. - **Host map** — every host and the peers it reached, edge thickness by flow count, force layout. - **East-west** — Internet traffic removed, so what is left is exactly what a segmentation policy is supposed to constrain. Paired with a table of accepted RDP / SMB / WinRM / SSH / database paths. - **Segments** — addresses grouped by /24, /16 or host, rendered both as a hierarchical graph and as a flow matrix punchcard. Every dot is a path that exists today; every empty cell is a boundary nothing crossed. - **Services** — which protocols actually carry the cross-boundary traffic. Usually a much shorter list than people expect. - **Lateral reach scoring** — how many internal hosts each machine reached, against the estate average in standard deviations, so an outlier surfaces without a hand-tuned threshold. ### Tabs everywhere they replace scrolling Eight of the nine dashboards are now tabbed. Nothing was removed; the same panels stopped being a two-thousand-pixel scroll. | Dashboard | Tabs | |---|---| | Firewall Overview | Summary · Collection health · Geography & changes | | Traffic Explorer | Flow map · Volume · Breakdown | | Segmentation Map | Host map · East-west · Segments · Services | | Host 360 | Activity · Peers & services · Processes · Changes | | Process Attribution | Process map · Hunting · Outbound & listeners | | Firewall Changes | Activity · Posture over time · Actors · Full history | | Threat Hunting | Reconnaissance · Command & control · Exposure · Data movement | | Firewall Posture | Compliance · Blind spots · Rule inventory | Peer Pivot and Traffic Investigator stay single-page on purpose: they are drilldown targets, and a drilldown lands on the first tab. ### More network graphs Beyond the segmentation map, the graph is used wherever a relationship reads better than a table: - **Beaconing map** (Threat Hunting) — hosts and the addresses they call back to. One external node with many host edges is either your management tooling or your incident. - **Exposure map** — which public addresses reach which of your hosts. - **Peer map** (Host 360) and **reach map** (Peer Pivot). - **Process to service map** (Process Attribution and Host 360). - **User to host change map** (Firewall Changes) — an account touching many hosts is either your automation or your problem. - **Host to risk map** (Posture) — which machines carry which rule risks. ### Timelines The 10.2 timeline visualisation, where a lane per category beats a stacked column: - Firewall Changes: change timeline by outcome, and an enable/disable timeline per host — a red mark is a window during which a host was unprotected. - Host 360: change timeline by category. - Threat Hunting: scan activity by intensity band. - Posture: posture drift over time. ### Trellis small multiples - Overview: blocked ratio as one colour-ranged gauge per host — an outlier is visible without reading a table. - Posture: compliance as a filler gauge per firewall profile. Public is usually the one that drifts. - Firewall Changes: change count per severity. - Traffic Explorer: one column chart per verdict. - Process Attribution: blocked events per binary. ### Conditional sections Sections that depend on optional data sources now disappear instead of sitting empty. Panels carry `hideWhenNoData`, and an **Optional sections** input removes their headers too. Affects the process attribution blocks in Host 360 and Threat Hunting, and the live posture panel in Host 360. ### Smaller 10.x touches - Row numbers on every investigation table. - Range-based cell colouring on the columns where a number carries a verdict: beaconing `jitter`, outbound `mb_out`, exposure `sources`, lateral `deviation`, segment `flows`. - Markdown tables in the release-notes-style panels and the documentation view. - Line chart acceleration applies automatically to the high-density time charts. ### Unchanged from 3.1.0 Every macro, field, eventtype, lookup, saved search, data model and view name is identical. The collection layer, the CIM mappings, the detections and the companion **TA-windows-firewall-posture** (still 1.0.0, still Splunk 9.0+, forwarder side) are untouched. Upgrading from 3.1.0 is a package replacement with no reconfiguration. ## 3.1.0 Three things this release is about: knowing **which binary** opened a connection, making the app **survive real data volumes**, and answering **"what is the state right now"** rather than only "what changed while we were watching". ### Added — process attribution - **Process Attribution view**. Windows Filtering Platform audit events (Security 5152/5156/5157, plus 5154/5155/5158/5159 for listeners) carry the full application path that `pfirewall.log` does not have. The app normalises them entirely in SPL, through the new `wfo_wfp` macro, so it never claims props on the shared `XmlWinEventLog:Security` sourcetype and never conflicts with Splunk_TA_windows or your existing Security collection. - New macros `wfo_wfp_index`, `wfo_wfp_base`, `wfo_wfp` and `wfo_network` (unified pfirewall + WFP). - Four detections: LOLBin with network activity, rare binary making network connections, new listening process, process repeatedly blocked outbound. - The setup page now takes a second index, because Security events almost never live in the same index as the firewall traffic log. ### Added — performance - **`Windows_Firewall_Observability` data model**, two datasets (Traffic, Changes), 48 fields. Acceleration ships **off** — that cost is your decision, not the app's. - The Overview now runs on `tstats` against that model. It works either way: with `summariesonly=false` (the shipped default) it searches raw data exactly as before; set the `wfo_summariesonly` macro — or answer "yes" on the setup page — once acceleration is on, and the same page reads summaries only. - New `is_noise` field, computed in props from the fixed non-routable, multicast, broadcast and reserved ranges. Unlike the `ip_whitelist` lookup, it is a data model field, so tstats panels can filter structural noise. The lookup stays as the tuning layer for your own organisation-specific ranges on the raw-search views. ### Added — investigation workflow - **Host 360**: one machine, everything — peers, services, processes, firewall state, configuration history, and its distinct-peer count against its own rolling 24-hour baseline expressed in standard deviations. - **Peer Pivot**: one IP address, everything — how far it reached into the estate, which ports, the timing regularity of the exchanges per host, and which processes talked to it. - Every table across the Overview, Traffic Explorer, Investigator, Threat Hunting and Posture views now drills into Host 360 or Peer Pivot instead of dumping you into a raw search, carrying the time range along. - Navigation regrouped into Traffic / Investigate / Configuration collections. ### Added — posture - **Firewall Posture view** plus the companion **TA-windows-firewall-posture** (separate package, forwarder side). Two read-only PowerShell inputs inventory the profile state, default actions, logging settings, log file health and the enabled rule set with a risk score. - This closes the blind spot the event stream cannot: a host whose firewall was already off before Splunk arrived produces no change event, and a host with drop logging disabled produces no traffic log at all — until now it was indistinguishable from a quiet host. - Four detections, including **Host Not Logging Dropped Packets**, which is the one that tells you an empty dashboard means nothing. ### Notes - Minimum platform is still Splunk 9.0. Dashboard Studio features that would have helped here — network graph, tabs, conditional panel visibility — need 10.x and were deliberately left out. - Nothing from 3.0.0 was removed. Existing macros, fields and view names are unchanged. ## 3.0.0 Major release. Collection, normalisation, dashboards and detections were all reworked. ### Fixed - **The setup page had no effect.** It wrote a macro named `windows_pfirewall_index` while every search of the app used `windows_firewall_index`. Whatever index you configured was ignored and all searches silently ran against `index=*`. Re-run the setup page once after upgrading. - **Field extraction shifted by one column on some Windows builds.** The positional `DELIMS` extraction assumed 18 columns; Windows Server 2016/2019 write 17 (no process id). Replaced by a regex extraction whose last group is optional, so both layouts are handled. - **Data loss after log rotation.** The four header lines of `pfirewall.log` are identical after every rotation, so Splunk computed the same CRC and resumed at the previous offset. `initCrcLength = 2048` now makes the CRC include real traffic lines. - **Header lines were indexed as events**, polluting every count. They are now routed to nullQueue. - Wrong CIM mapping: `protocol` carried the transport value. It now carries the network-layer value (`ip` / `ipv6`); `transport` keeps `tcp` / `udp` / `icmp`. - Profile bitmask decoding only handled Public, Private and None. Domain and the combined values (3, 5, 6, 7, 2147483647) are decoded too. - Typos in the vendor product name ("Windows Defender Firewal"). - The `windows_firewall_event_id` lookup returned up to nine rows for a single EventID, turning `Description` into a multivalue field. It is now one row per EventID. ### Added - **Five Dashboard Studio views**, responsive grid layout, dark theme: - *Firewall Overview* — collection health, allowed vs blocked volume, blocked ratio, noisiest services, top talkers, firewall state per host, world map of external destinations. - *Traffic Explorer* — two-level flow map (host → service → verdict), volume in connections and in bytes, services, remote peers, activity punchcard. - *Traffic Investigator* — filterable tables with geo enrichment and service resolution. - *Firewall Changes* — severity-ranked audit trail, change timeline, authors, firewall state. - *Threat Hunting* — port scans, network sweeps, beaconing, Internet exposure, data movement. - **Sixteen saved searches**: 15 detections (all disabled by default) and 6 reports. Highlights: firewall disabled, default inbound action set to allow, service stopped, policy reset, inbound allow rule created, rule deleted, policy change burst, port scan, network sweep, excessive denied outbound, C2 beaconing, data exfiltration, exposed service, administrative protocol exposed, host stopped reporting. - **Service resolution**: `dest_service` is derived from the destination port and transport through a new lookup of 81 common services. - **Internal / external scoping**: `src_scope` and `dest_scope` let every search separate lateral traffic from Internet exposure. The ranges are configurable from the setup page. - New macros `wfo_traffic`, `wfo_changes` and `wfo_internal_ip(ip)`. - Severity ranking of configuration events (`severity`), plus `firewall_enabled`, `default_inbound_action`, `default_outbound_action` and `setting_name`. - CIM **Change** data model compliance for the configuration events: `action` now uses the allowed set (created / modified / deleted), with `object`, `object_category`, `object_attrs`, `object_path` and `result`. - Optional input stanzas for per-profile log files, the ConnectionSecurity channel and the Windows Filtering Platform audit events. - A rewritten setup page: validation, live feedback, index list and internal ranges, no silent failure. - A rewritten documentation view: installation, GPO and PowerShell activation, field reference, tuning and a troubleshooting table. ### Changed - The generic eventtype `traffic`, which was exported globally, is replaced by `windows_firewall_traffic`. The CIM tags are unchanged, so the Network Traffic data model keeps populating. - The 16th column of `pfirewall.log` is named `packet_info` instead of `field16`. `info` still holds SEND / RECEIVE. - `whitelist_ip_ranges.csv` now covers the full multicast and reserved ranges (`224.0.0.0/4`, `240.0.0.0/4`) instead of a few /8 subsets. - Minimum platform is Splunk 9.0. ## 2.0.0 Initial Splunkbase release: data inputs, field extractions, CIM Network Traffic knowledge objects, sankey and table dashboards, firewall change history.


Description:
This App was designed to Collect, parse, normalise and visualise Windows Defender Firewall activity: the connection log (pfirewall.log), the configuration and policy change events, the Windows Filtering Platform audit events that attribute a connection to the binary that opened it, and - with the companion TA-windows-firewall-posture - the current configuration state of every host. Built for Dashboard Studio 10.4: tabbed dashboards, network graphs for east-west and beaconing maps, timelines, trellis small multiples and conditional sections. Ships hardened data inputs, a version-tolerant field extraction, CIM compliant knowledge objects for the Network Traffic and Change data models, an accelerable data model, nine dashboards and twenty-four detections and reports.

Provider responses are evaluated against configurable thresholds, and malicious findings can automatically update the notable event urgency, add enrichment evidence as an ES comment, and trigger an email notification. DV IOC Enrichment addresses the operational overhead of manually investigating repeated indicators while preventing unnecessary API usage through configurable caching, exclusion rules, provider-specific quota controls, and multi-key rotation. Each provider operates independently. If one provider becomes unavailable or reaches its quota, enrichment continues through the remaining providers. Temporarily incomplete events can be retried when provider capacity becomes available again. The app includes: - Automatic enrichment of Splunk ES notable events - VirusTotal support for IP, domain, URL, and hash indicators - AbuseIPDB support for public IP reputation - MISP support for IP, domain, URL, and hash attribute matches - AlienVault OTX support for IP, domain, URL, and hash pulse intelligence - Configurable provider-specific thresholds - Multiple API keys with quota-aware rotation - Per-provider request and quota controls - Reusable enrichment cache with configurable TTL - Exact, CIDR, IP range, and domain suffix exclusions - Independent provider fallback and retry handling - Automatic urgency updates and ES comments - Optional email notifications - Operational dashboard with provider evidence drilldown - Read-only application Health Check - Structured internal logging
